# title: Fixture guide to land care after wildfire

Hydrophobic soils after fire
Severe, slow-moving fires can bake a waxy water-repellent coating into the soil surface.
To test for it, place a drop of water on bare soil and watch whether the drop beads up
instead of soaking in. Repeat the test at one-inch depths to find how thick the layer is.
Breaking this water repellent layer is essential before seeding so that rain can soak
into the soil and seeds can germinate. Rake or harrow through the layer on small areas.

Straw mulching on burned slopes
Spread certified weed-free straw mulch at 1-2 tons/acre on burned slopes before the first
fall rains. Crimp or tackify the straw on windy sites so it stays in place.
In the fixture trial, straw mulch reduced sediment yield by 50-70% during the first winter
after the fire on slopes steeper than 30 percent.
Mulch is less useful on gentle slopes where little soil moves.

Biochar for sandy soils
Biochar made from forest thinning slash can be worked into coarse, sandy soils to hold water.
In a greenhouse study, biochar applied at 5-10% by volume raised the water holding capacity
of a sandy loam by roughly one fifth compared with unamended soil.
Fine clay soils showed little change, so match the amendment to soil texture.

Cover crops through winter
Cereal rye planted right after harvest protects bare cropland soil through winter storms.
The roots hold soil in place, and the residue adds organic matter when it is turned in.
Growers in the fixture survey reported less wind erosion on fields kept covered all winter.

References
